passage: Vishal, you look like the aunties cornered you at the engagement. Come, sit with your Himani bua. When I was twenty-one, every wedding was a trial. "Himani, still not married? Your cousin has two children already." One lady even brought a boy's photo in her handbag. I used to smile, go to the bathroom and cry. I felt like a train running late on somebody else's timetable. Then at my cousin's mehendi, old Pinky-mausi asked again. I was tired. I held her hand and said, "Mausi, I know you ask because you care. When there's news, you'll be the first I call." She laughed and patted my cheek, and that was it. I married at thirty-one, to someone I chose. The aunties survived. So will you, beta. Be kind to them, but keep your own clock.

passage: I'm Yusuf, Kiran's Abbu, and I'll tell you what I saw this year, since you asked. My son is twenty-five. In twelve months he has had three jobs: the bank, a start-up, now some design studio. He still lives in his old room. At his age I was married and had a scooter loan. Every time he packed a new lunch box for a new office, I felt my chest tighten. One night I was ready to tell him he was wasting his life. Instead, I don't know why, I asked him, "What did you like in the last one?" He talked for an hour. About colours, about a client who cried happy tears. I don't know what he feels inside, not fully. But he didn't look lost. He looked like someone still searching. My brother says young people now take longer. Maybe. So now I ask more than I tell.

passage: Vaibhav, you think your parents are too hard on you for moving back home? Let me tell you about my Ravi. At twenty-six he'd left two jobs in two years and was sleeping till ten in his old room. I was a school principal; I had opinions about everything. One Sunday I wrote him a long letter listing where he was going wrong. I never gave it. Because that morning I heard him on the phone, calmly helping his friend through a panic, and I thought, I don't actually know this man. So I tore up the letter and asked him to walk with me to the market. I asked what he was afraid of. He said, "Letting you down, Amma." Took him three more years to find his work. He's a good architect now. Gargi learnt late that questions open doors verdicts slam shut.

passage:
Dear Mehak,
You asked if I feel like a grown-up now that I'm twenty-four. Honestly? Not on my birthday. Not when the cake came out. But in small moments, lately, yes.
Last month I booked my own dentist appointment and actually went, even though I hate the drill. I made a spreadsheet of my spending, which is terrifying and very boring. I promised Ma I'd visit every second weekend, and I've kept it five times in a row. I told my manager I needed help on a report instead of pretending.
None of it is dramatic. It's just me doing things I used to wait for someone else to do. I think being an adult is built from little bricks like that. Some weeks I drop a brick. Then I pick it up.
Write back and tell me your bricks.
Vinita

passage: I've shared a flat with my cousin Sangeeta for a year now, so I've watched it happen up close. When she moved to Pune at twenty-three, her mother still booked her doctor visits from Nagpur and reminded her about the rent. Sangeeta would forget the gas cylinder and call home in a panic. Then, slowly, things changed. She put a calendar on the fridge. She started calling the gas agency herself, a bit stiff on the phone at first. She sat with a notebook every Sunday, writing figures, frowning. When her friend's wedding clashed with a work deadline, she finished the report on Friday night so she could keep both. I don't know what goes on in her head. But last week I heard her say to her mother, "No, Ma, I've already booked it." She sounded almost surprised. I think she was.

11:40 p.m., Saturday
Fought with Amma AGAIN about the 9 p.m. rule. I said everyone else can stay till ten, Yash's parents don't even text him. She said Yash's parents are not my parents. I said some stuff. She said some stuff. I slammed the door.

I don't hate her. I just need some of me to be only mine.

Tuesday night
Lakshmi used to jump on my bed after school and talk until I begged for quiet. She's fourteen now. Today I asked how the science exhibition went. "Fine." Who was there? "People." Then her door closed.
I sat in the kitchen feeling stupidly hurt, like I'd been dropped by a friend. Part of me wanted to march in and demand answers. Part of me wanted to stop trying and let her see how it feels.
I did neither. I made her favourite lemon rice and left a note: "Here if you want to tell me anything. No lectures." Around ten, she came out for water and said, "The judge liked our model." Just that. I said, "I'm glad." I didn't ask more.
Ankita, you are the adult here. Be the door that stays open.

passage: Looking back now, the thing I remember about my first term in Delhi isn't the classes. It's the second Sunday. I'd done well all week: opened a bank account, found the laundry, argued with the auto driver and won. I felt tall. Then in the mess they served rajma, and it smelt nothing like Minakshi-maasi's. I went back to my room and cried into my pillow for an hour. I was eighteen and embarrassed; I thought real adults don't cry over beans. I didn't tell anyone. That night I called home, just to hear the TV in the background, my father coughing, my maasi scolding the dog. I didn't even say I was sad. I just listened. Only later did I understand that the ache wasn't weakness. It meant the people back home were still part of me. I'm Rajni, and I still call on Sundays.
